characters.name: Joshua

genealogy.note: Josh 1:1: 'Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' minister.' Called 'Jehoshua'/'Oshea' and given his tribal affiliation (Ephraim) only outside this book (Numbers 13:8,16) — not stated within the text of Joshua itself, so not asserted here as this book's own claim.

verses.note: Commissioned by the LORD after Moses' death; charged to be strong and of good courage.
Leads Israel across the Jordan on dry ground as the priests bear the ark.
Encounters 'the captain of the LORD's host' near Jericho and is told to remove his shoe, 'for the place whereon thou standest is holy.'
Leads the march and trumpet-blowing around Jericho until its walls fall.
Commands the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Ajalon.
Farewell charge to Israel's leaders in his old age.
Renews the covenant at Shechem: 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.'
Dies and is buried in Timnathserah in mount Ephraim.

ageEvents.event: Death, described as 'the servant of the LORD'

funFacts: Called 'Jehoshua'/'Oshea' in other passages (Numbers 13:16) — not within Joshua's own text.
At his death he is called 'the servant of the LORD' (Josh 24:29), a title the book elsewhere reserves for Moses (Josh 1:1).

characters.name: Rahab

genealogy.note: Her father's household (unnamed individually) is spared alongside her, Josh 6:23,25. Matthew 1:5 (KJV spelling 'Rachab') later names a 'Rachab' as Salmon's wife and Boaz's mother, and this is widely identified with this Rahab — but the long gap between the conquest and David's era makes the timeline debated among scholars, and Joshua's own text says nothing about a marriage or descendants; not asserted here as Joshua's own claim.

verses.note: Hides the two spies sent by Joshua and hangs a scarlet cord/line from her window per their agreement.
Spared with her household when Jericho is destroyed; 'and she dwelleth in Israel even unto this day.'

funFacts: Explicitly called 'Rahab the harlot' in the KJV text itself (Josh 2:1, 6:17,25).
The two spies she hides are never named in the text (Josh 2:1).

characters.name: Achan

genealogy.note: Full stated line: 'Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah' (Josh 7:1,18). His unnamed sons and daughters are put to death with him (Josh 7:24) but are not individually named, so no separate character entries are given for them. Zerah is a common name reused elsewhere in scripture (e.g. Zerah son of Judah and Tamar, Genesis 38) — not claimed to be the same person here.

verses.note: Introduced as having 'committed a trespass in the accursed thing' from Jericho's spoil.
Identified by lot, confesses to taking a Babylonish garment, silver, and a wedge of gold; stoned and burned in the valley of Achor.
Retrospectively invoked as a warning: 'Did not Achan the son of Zerah commit a trespass...and that man perished not alone in his iniquity.'

funFacts: 1 Chronicles 2:7 calls him 'Achar, the troubler of Israel' — an explicit wordplay on the place-name 'Achor' (trouble) from Josh 7:26.

characters.name: The Gibeonites

genealogy.note: Represented collectively — no individual Gibeonite is named in Joshua 9-10. Treated here as a single narrative unit per this index's convention for an undifferentiated named group.

verses.note: Disguise themselves as travelers from a distant land to trick Israel into a covenant of peace; once discovered, made 'hewers of wood and drawers of water' rather than destroyed, because Israel had sworn by the LORD.
Besieged by the five-king coalition for making peace with Israel, prompting Joshua's rescue march and the long day at Gibeon.

funFacts: Their trickery worked specifically because Israel 'asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD' (Josh 9:14).

characters.name: Adonizedek

genealogy.note: No family is named for him. King of Jerusalem.

verses.note: Organizes a five-king Amorite coalition (naming Hoham, Piram, Japhia, and Debir individually) to besiege Gibeon for making peace with Israel.
Hides with the other four kings in the cave at Makkedah; captured, executed, and hanged on trees until evening.

funFacts: His name ('lord of righteousness') invites comparison to 'Melchizedek' ('king of righteousness'), an earlier king of the same city in Genesis 14:18 — a name-pattern similarity only; the text nowhere states a family or identity link between them.

characters.name: Hoham
characters.perkNote: One of the four kings Adonizedek summons against Gibeon; captured and executed alongside him (Josh 10:3,5,16-27).

genealogy.note: No family named.

verses.note: Named as king of Hebron, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

characters.name: Piram
characters.perkNote: One of the four kings Adonizedek summons against Gibeon; captured and executed alongside him (Josh 10:3,5,16-27).

genealogy.note: No family named.

verses.note: Named as king of Jarmuth, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

characters.name: Japhia
characters.perkNote: One of the four kings Adonizedek summons against Gibeon; captured and executed alongside him (Josh 10:3,5,16-27).

genealogy.note: No family named here. NAMING COLLISION: 'Japhia' is also the name of one of David's sons born at Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:15; 1 Chronicles 3:7, 14:6) — an entirely different, much later person; flagged explicitly.

verses.note: Named as king of Lachish, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

characters.name: Debir
characters.perkNote: One of the four kings Adonizedek summons against Gibeon; captured and executed alongside him (Josh 10:3,5,16-27).

genealogy.note: No family named. NAMING COLLISION (within this very book): 'Debir' is used here as a personal name (king of Eglon), but 'Debir' is also a Canaanite city in the hill country of Judah, formerly called Kirjathsepher, later taken by Othniel (Josh 10:38-39; 15:15-17) — same word, two distinct referents; flagged explicitly.

verses.note: Named as king of Eglon, summoned by Adonizedek.
Brought out of the cave at Makkedah and executed with the other four kings.

characters.name: Jabin

genealogy.note: No family named. NAMING COLLISION: a different 'Jabin king of Hazor' appears generations later in Judges 4:2,17,23-24 as the oppressor defeated via Deborah, Barak, and Jael. Whether this reflects the same royal/dynastic name reused at Hazor or two unrelated figures who merely share a name and city-title is debated by scholars; this index treats the two accounts as describing two separate figures.

verses.note: Assembles a northern coalition of kings at the waters of Merom; defeated by Joshua, and Hazor, 'the head of all those kingdoms,' is burned.

funFacts: Hazor is the only city among the defeated northern coalition that Israel burns (Josh 11:13).

characters.name: Caleb

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: this Caleb ('the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite,' Josh 14:6,14) is a distinct figure from 'Caleb the son of Hezron,' documented separately in Judah's tribal genealogy at 1 Chronicles 2:18-19,42-49 — a different father and lineage, with no stated connection to Jephunneh or 'the Kenezite.' The two share only a name; this index does not merge them. Separately, his brother Othniel is called 'the son of Kenaz' (Josh 15:17); whether Caleb's own 'Kenezite' designation reflects the same Kenaz as a shared father or is a broader clan/tribal label is not made explicit by the text and is left unresolved here rather than silently decided.

verses.note: Claims Hebron at Gilgal, citing Moses' oath after the spy mission from Kadeshbarnea forty-five years earlier.
Given Hebron; offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever takes Kirjathsepher (Debir).

ageEvents.event: Sent by Moses from Kadeshbarnea to spy out the land
Claims his inheritance at Hebron, forty-five years after the spying mission

funFacts: Explicitly called 'the Kenezite' (Josh 14:6,14), a clan designation elsewhere associated with Edom (cf. Genesis 36:11,15) rather than a native Israelite line of Judah by that title alone — yet he receives a full inheritance within Judah's territory.

characters.name: Achsah
characters.perkNote: Caleb's daughter, offered as the prize for whoever takes Kirjathsepher (Josh 15:16); after marrying Othniel, she requests and receives 'the upper springs and the nether springs' from her father — the source of this tier's name.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given in the text beyond her marriage to Othniel.

verses.note: Married to Othniel after he takes Kirjathsepher; asks Caleb for springs of water in addition to a south land.

characters.name: Othniel
characters.perkNote: Takes Kirjathsepher (Debir) in battle, winning Achsah's hand per Caleb's offer (Josh 15:17).

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb' (Josh 15:17) — the KJV wording is ambiguous whether 'the brother of Caleb' modifies Othniel or Kenaz. Judges 3:9 later reads 'Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother,' which most naturally makes Othniel and Caleb brothers, but some readings still take Othniel as Kenaz's son and thus Caleb's nephew. Hedged, not resolved, per this index's rule against silently deciding textual cruxes.

verses.note: Takes Kirjathsepher and receives Achsah as wife.

funFacts: Later becomes Israel's first judge, delivering the nation from Chushanrishathaim (Judges 3:9-11) — outside the scope of Joshua itself.

characters.name: Mahlah

genealogy.note: Full stated line for her father: 'Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh' (Josh 17:3). Named first among her sisters in both Numbers 26:33 and Joshua 17:3. The five daughters act and speak as an undifferentiated group in the text, so only Mahlah is given a full manager entry here, with her sisters as submanagers per this index's convention for undifferentiated named groups.

verses.note: Comes with her sisters before Eleazar, Joshua, and the princes, citing the LORD's earlier command to Moses; receives an inheritance among their father's brethren.

funFacts: Their claim was already granted in principle in Numbers 27:1-11 and reaffirmed in Numbers 36; Joshua 17:3-6 records its actual fulfillment in the land.

characters.name: Noah
characters.perkNote: One of Zelophehad's five daughters named alongside Mahlah in the inheritance claim (Josh 17:3).

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: this 'Noah' (a daughter of Zelophehad) shares her name in the KJV with the flood patriarch Noah (Genesis 5-9) — the same English spelling represents two unrelated figures; flagged explicitly.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

characters.name: Hoglah
characters.perkNote: One of Zelophehad's five daughters named alongside Mahlah in the inheritance claim (Josh 17:3).

genealogy.note: Possible name-echo (not asserted as a connection): a town called 'Bethhoglah' ('house of Hoglah') sits on the Judah/Benjamin border within this same book (Josh 15:6; 18:19,21). The text never links the town's name to this daughter; flagged only as a shared root worth noting, not a claimed identification.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

characters.name: Milcah
characters.perkNote: One of Zelophehad's five daughters named alongside Mahlah in the inheritance claim (Josh 17:3).

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION: shares her name with Milcah, wife of Nahor (Abraham's brother), named repeatedly in Genesis (11:29; 22:20,23; 24:15,24,47) — a different, much earlier figure; flagged explicitly.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

characters.name: Tirzah
characters.perkNote: One of Zelophehad's five daughters named alongside Mahlah in the inheritance claim (Josh 17:3).

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION (within this very book): shares her name with the Canaanite city of Tirzah, whose king is listed among the 31 defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:24), and which later becomes an early capital of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 14:17; 15:21,33) — same word, two distinct referents; flagged explicitly.

verses.note: Named among Zelophehad's five daughters.

characters.name: Cities of Refuge
characters.deliveredBy: Joshua, relaying the command the LORD had earlier given through Moses (Josh 20:1-2; cf. Numbers 35:9-15, Deuteronomy 19:1-13).
characters.purpose: Establishes six cities (three west and three east of the Jordan) where a person who kills another 'unawares and unwittingly' (Josh 20:3) may flee from the avenger of blood and receive a fair hearing before the congregation, remaining safe until the death of the high priest then serving — teaching that unintentional killing is judged differently from murder, and that justice requires due process rather than immediate vengeance.

verses.note: Purpose and procedure of the cities of refuge.
Names the six cities: Kedesh, Shechem, and Kirjatharba (Hebron) west of Jordan; Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan east of Jordan.

funFacts: The exact KJV phrase is 'unawares and unwittingly' (Josh 20:3) — not the reverse order sometimes seen in paraphrase.

characters.name: Levitical Cities
characters.deliveredBy: The heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites, who came to Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the tribal fathers' houses (Josh 21:1-3), fulfilling what 'the LORD commanded by the hand of Moses' (Josh 21:2; cf. Numbers 35:1-8).
characters.purpose: Assigns the Levites forty-eight cities with surrounding pasture lands out of the other tribes' inheritances, since the Levites received no territorial inheritance of their own (cf. Josh 13:33) — teaching that the priestly/Levitical calling is itself their portion, with the LORD as their inheritance, while still providing practically for their material needs through the rest of the nation.

verses.note: The Levites' request, made per the LORD's command through Moses.
Summary: forty-eight cities with their suburbs given to the Levites.

characters.name: Phinehas

genealogy.note: Josh 22:13,32: 'Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest.' NAMING COLLISION: a different Phinehas — son of Eli, a priest at Shiloh and brother of Hophni — appears later in 1 Samuel 1-4 (e.g. 1 Sam 1:3; 4:4,11,17) and is explicitly a separate lineage (Eli's line), not stated to descend from this Phinehas or from Eleazar; flagged explicitly.

verses.note: Sent with ten tribal princes to confront Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh over the altar they built by the Jordan.
Satisfied by their explanation that the altar was meant as a witness, not for sacrifice; reports back and war is averted.

funFacts: Already introduced earlier in Numbers 25:7-13 (zeal against Baalpeor, granted a covenant of an everlasting priesthood) — that episode predates Joshua and is not itself part of this book's text; only his identity and lineage carry forward here.

genealogy.note: His descent from Aaron is common scriptural knowledge (e.g. Exodus 6:23,25; Numbers 20:26-28) rather than something restated within Joshua's own text, so it is noted here, not asserted as a claim made by Joshua itself. NAMING COLLISION: distinct from other Eleazars in scripture, e.g. Eleazar son of Abinadab, who kept the ark at Kirjathjearim (1 Samuel 7:1), and Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite, one of David's three mighty men (2 Samuel 23:9); flagged explicitly.

verses.note: Co-presides with Joshua and the tribal heads over the distribution of Canaan's inheritance by lot.
Receives Zelophehad's daughters' inheritance claim alongside Joshua.
Receives the Levites' request for cities.
Dies; buried in a hill belonging to Phinehas his son in mount Ephraim.

genealogyLists.thirty_one_kings_ch12: Joshua 12 lists 31 kings defeated on the west side of Jordan under Joshua (12:7-24), on top of Sihon and Og defeated earlier under Moses east of Jordan (12:1-6). Beyond the five kings of the ch10 coalition (Adonizedek, Hoham, Piram, Japhia, Debir of Eglon) and Jabin of Hazor (ch11) — all given full entries above — the remaining roughly 25 kings are identified only by the city they ruled, with no individual action differentiated in the text; not given separate character entries.
genealogyLists.sihon_and_og_ch12: Joshua 12:1-6 recaps Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, kings defeated earlier under Moses — their narrative belongs to Numbers 21, referenced here only in summary.
genealogyLists.tribal_boundary_and_town_lists_ch13_15_1: Chapters 13 and 15-19 give detailed tribal territory boundaries and town-name lists for Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh (ch13), Judah (ch15), Ephraim (ch16), the rest of Manasseh (ch17), Benjamin (ch18), and Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan (ch19) — almost entirely geographic (place names and boundary markers) with no individual personal action attached, beyond Caleb (ch14-15) and Zelophehad's daughters (ch17:3-6), both already given full entries above.
genealogyLists.ten_princes_ch22: Joshua 22:13-14 sends Phinehas 'and with him ten princes, of each chief house a prince throughout all the tribes' to confront the eastern tribes over the altar of witness; none of the ten is individually named in the text.
genealogyLists.reuben_gad_manasseh_respondents_ch22: The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh who built the altar of witness (Josh 22:10-34) respond and are quoted collectively; no individual leader on their side is named within Joshua 22 itself (contrast Numbers 32, which names some of their earlier leaders in a different episode).
genealogyLists.unnamed_spies_ch2: The 'two men to spy secretly' whom Joshua sends to Jericho, and whom Rahab hides (Josh 2:1), are never named.
genealogyLists.twelve_men_ch3_4: The twelve men chosen 'out of every tribe a man' to carry stones from the dry Jordan bed (Josh 3:12; 4:2-8) are not individually named, unlike the comparable tribal-representative list in Numbers 34.

notes:
Second-pass (post-adversarial-fact-check) redraft of Joshua's character index, built from scratch per project methodology. Corrects the sole flagged first-draft issue: Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenezite is now explicitly distinguished, in his genealogy.note, from the unrelated 'Caleb the son of Hezron' documented separately in Judah's genealogy at 1 Chronicles 2:18-19,42-49 (different father, different lineage, name-only overlap).

Additional naming collisions proactively caught and flagged during this pass, none present in the original issue list: Jabin king of Hazor (Josh 11) vs. a later 'Jabin king of Hazor' in Judges 4; Phinehas son of Eleazar (Josh 22) vs. Phinehas son of Eli (1 Samuel 1-4); Eleazar the priest (son of Aaron) vs. Eleazar son of Abinadab (1 Sam 7:1) and Eleazar the Ahohite (2 Sam 23:9); Debir king of Eglon (a person, Josh 10:3) vs. Debir the city (Josh 10:38-39, 15:15) within this very book; Japhia king of Lachish (Josh 10) vs. Japhia son of David (2 Sam 5:15); and, among Zelophehad's five daughters (Josh 17:3-6): Noah vs. the flood patriarch Noah, and Milcah vs. Milcah wife of Nahor (Genesis 11:29) — two names the project's own methodology explicitly lists as repeat offenders, both genuinely reused here. Tirzah (daughter) vs. Tirzah (city, Josh 12:24, later a northern-kingdom capital) also flagged, and a lighter Hoglah/Bethhoglah name-echo is noted without asserting a connection.

Zelophehad's five daughters — the exact scenario used as the methodology's own worked example for undifferentiated named groups — are handled as one major (Mahlah, named first in both Numbers 26:33 and Josh 17:3) plus four loyalty-boost submanagers, rather than five separate majors. Othniel's relation to Caleb ('the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb,' Josh 15:17, clarified but not fully disambiguated by Judges 3:9) is hedged as textually ambiguous rather than silently resolved. Geographic-only material — the ~25 undifferentiated kings of ch12 beyond the five of ch10 and Jabin of ch11, the tribal boundary/town lists of ch13 and 15-19, and the unnamed spies/princes/tribal representatives of ch2, 3-4, and 22 — is captured in genealogyLists rather than invented as individual characters, per the book-specific guidance that land allotments are mostly geographic unless a person acts. All managerId/parentManagerId references were re-checked against the characters array; no character holds both a scribeTier and a parentManagerId.
